segments.title: Opening and sound level check at Miller's home
segments.summary: Allen announces the date, place and participants and Miller plays trumpet to set recording levels.

segments.title: Edward Clem's street style and funeral playing
segments.summary: Miller says he heard but never played with Clem and Manuel Perez; he discusses how Clem played in brass bands, parades and funerals.

segments.title: Manuel Perez's playing: funeral marches, regular marches and jazz on the way back
segments.summary: Miller explains that funeral marches were played straight, marches were played from the music, and jazz numbers came on the return; Perez played melody, rather high.

segments.title: Bunk playing the excursion and Miller hearing him as a boy
segments.summary: Miller describes hopping a train to hear a band on an excursion to Homer, Louisiana, and watching the cornetist play one piece repeatedly.

segments.title: Kimball's style, reading and a tune
segments.summary: Miller describes cornetist Kimball as a strong reader who played show and street music, and tries to recall his feature tune; the machine is paused briefly.

segments.title: Buddy Petit in brass bands: second trumpet, solos coming back, and choosing his own men
segments.summary: Petit played second trumpet in the street and took solos on the return; Petit, Rene, Chris Kelly and Miller never played with the old established bands like the Tuxedo.

segments.title: How often jump-up bands played funerals and who hired them
segments.summary: Miller says about four funerals a month, bands going out of town on weekends, Monday-night dances, and clubs and societies hiring leaders for funerals.

segments.title: White clubs and burials with music
segments.summary: Allen asks whether the white carnival clubs buried members with music; Miller says they played carnival and Mardi Gras and would have used white bands.

segments.title: Rene's high notes on slow hymns and dirges
segments.summary: Miller says Rene played the lead and reached up for high notes at the end of a slow piece.

segments.title: Country brass bands and funerals around Paul Rocher
segments.summary: Miller says a country band led by Paul Rocher played the same marches, hymns and jump-back music as New Orleans bands.

segments.title: Chicago: no street funerals, blowing taps
segments.summary: In Chicago Miller played the street only for the Elks convention and blew taps for burials, with Kelly and Jimmy Wade.

segments.title: Blues come into the street bands after a Zulu funeral
segments.summary: Miller recalls that he, Black Benny, Henry Martin and others played blues up-tempo on the way back from a funeral, after which all the bands did; dated about 1923-24.

segments.title: Returning in 1919 and working with Duck Ernest and Jack Carey
segments.summary: Miller says on his return in 1919 he played with Duck Ernest and then Jack Carey, who also paraded; they discuss Carey's earlier band affiliations.

segments.title: Black Benny's bass drum and how blues in the street started
segments.summary: Miller praises Black Benny's bass drumming and says Henry Martin and Black Benny started playing blues on the street.

segments.title: Personnel of the band that played blues in the street
segments.summary: Miller and Allen try to name the trombones, baritone, alto, clarinet and trumpet players in that band, including Pills and Eddie Jackson.

segments.title: Baritone horn in the brass bands and its disappearance
segments.summary: Miller praises one baritone player's carrying sound and notes that baritones are rarely seen now.

segments.title: Louis Dumaine and Pajot: brass-band arrangements and playing
segments.summary: They talk about Dumaine's hymn and march arrangements for the Eureka and Tuxedo bands, and whether he was a hot trumpet player.

segments.title: Burial societies and insurance, and who is buried with music
segments.summary: Allen asks how burial societies pay for bands, age limits, junior divisions, whether women or young people are buried with music, and passing-the-hat funerals.

segments.title: Playing with Ma Rainey, 1927-28
segments.summary: Miller explains he played with Ma Rainey from late 1927 to mid 1928, left her ill in Milwaukee, and had come on the road with a tent show that fell apart.

segments.title: First bands in New Orleans: Duck Ernest and Jack Carey
segments.summary: Miller recalls his boyhood friend who played alto and then lists Duck Ernest and Jack Carey as his first bands, with Carey for dance music.

segments.title: Celestin and the guitarist poisoned in Jack Carey's band
segments.summary: Miller says he only played second trumpet for Celestin occasionally, then tells of Carey's handsome guitarist.

segments.title: The trumpeter Robert Taylor who kicked a woman and was paralyzed
segments.summary: Miller tells how Robert Taylor, who had played with blues singers, kicked a woman and was afterward paralyzed; Zander asks if hoodoo was involved.

segments.title: Hoodoo stories, Buddy Petit's spit trick and a bootlegger woman
segments.summary: Miller describes belief in charms and tells of Buddy Petit winning a job with seeds and spitting, plus a woman bootlegger in Mobile, and the Cracker Jack drug store.

segments.title: Ma Rainey's brother and a stomping trombonist
segments.summary: They talk about Ma Rainey's brother possibly being in town and about a man who stomped while talking.

segments.title: Clarinetist Bubba Green and the Amos bands
segments.summary: Allen asks if Miller knows Bubba Green, who may have played with Amos Riley or Amos White.

segments.title: Trumpet rattle trouble and tape pause
segments.summary: Miller and Allen pause to sort out a rattle in the trumpet.

segments.title: George McCollum, Shots and Wooden Joe compared
segments.summary: Miller describes McCollum as a classical player and compares Shots, Buddy and Wooden Joe as lead or Armstrong-style players.

segments.title: Lee Collins's fingering and how Armstrong played when Miller arrived
segments.summary: They discuss Lee Collins's unusual fingering and his attempts to play like Armstrong.

segments.title: Buddy Petit holding long notes
segments.summary: Miller says Buddy Petit could hold a note long, like F, though not high.

segments.title: Tommy Ladnier and Joe Alba known only in Chicago
segments.summary: Miller says he first saw Ladnier and a second musician in Chicago and comments on their records.

segments.title: King Oliver's plunger and Coca-Cola bottle muting
segments.summary: Miller talks about Oliver playing open horn, plunger and Coca-Cola bottle and being loud, and tries it; the machine is paused.

segments.title: Miller's own fast-fingering style
segments.summary: Miller says he was called the fast finger, did not learn it from anyone, and mentions his feature piece.

segments.title: The finger-style feature and who else played that way
segments.summary: Miller recalls a feature learned from another player and says Oliver, Kimball, Clem and the Smith brothers played in that way.

segments.title: Did Buddy Petit play that style?
segments.summary: Miller says Buddy played a nice horn and got more tone, but is unsure about this style.

segments.title: Stop time and tap dancers; cutting notes
segments.summary: Miller explains that stop time was made for tap dancers, that he played Sweet Suit behind them, and that cut notes do not fit a hot solo.

segments.title: Rene's high endings and his records
segments.summary: Miller says Rene's endings went an octave higher and that his records were disappointing; they discuss musicians who hold back their best material.

segments.title: King Oliver's baby cry and Robert Taylor's preaching trumpet
segments.summary: Miller has not heard Oliver do the crying baby but describes Robert Taylor's preaching call-and-response trumpet.

segments.title: Origins of stop time and George Boyd's piece Number One
segments.summary: Miller says stop time began with tap dancers and describes George Boyd's piece with band stops.

segments.chapter: Making up numbers, bop and technique
segments.title: Bands making up their own numbers; Banana Peeling and trio sections
segments.summary: Miller says bands composed pieces so rivals could not top them, and tries Buddy's Banana Peeling, high society and Panama Rag trios.

segments.chapter: Making up numbers, bop and technique
segments.title: Lip swelling and trumpet players who played low
segments.summary: Miller blames lip swelling for missed notes and answers a question about low-register trumpeters.

segments.chapter: Making up numbers, bop and technique
segments.title: Faso's brushes and the wallet on the snare drum
segments.summary: Miller tells how a drummer named Faso played soft with brushes, a quilt and a wallet on the snare, and they compare with loud modern playing.

segments.chapter: Making up numbers, bop and technique
segments.title: Miller plays a bop piece
segments.summary: Miller plays a bop number and they discuss it.

segments.chapter: Making up numbers, bop and technique
segments.title: Playing bop for a show: Bones and billet pieces
segments.summary: Miller says he did not like the music but had it written out for a show, naming Bones; he then rests his lip.

segments.title: Hot and reading clarinet players: George Boyd, Mealy Barnes, Picou
segments.summary: Miller ranks clarinetists, noting who read and who got off, including George Boyd, Mealy Barnes, Picou and Zeb.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet and the 1925 band with Johnny and Baby Dodds
segments.summary: Miller recalls playing with Bechet and says his 1925 band included Ory, Dodds and Lorenzo Staulz.

segments.title: Forgotten fingering, two clarinets in brass bands, and the arrival of the saxophone
segments.summary: Miller notes old bands used two clarinets and that he had never seen a saxophone before leaving in 1917.

segments.title: Sam Dutrey and trombonists Honore and Dick O'Hara
segments.summary: They sort out the Dutrey brothers and Miller recalls trombonists who played with him in Chicago.

segments.title: George Washington, Earl Humphrey and the fastest trombone players
segments.summary: Miller praises George Washington as a fast trombonist and says Earl Humphrey was a wizard; he does not know what became of Washington.

segments.title: First blues gig, Tony, Chinese and Udell
segments.summary: Miller recalls his first paid night playing blues for fifty cents and half-remembered musicians he met.

segments.title: Chicago's Plantation and the great drummers, including the stick juggler
segments.summary: Miller names drummers, praising one who juggled eight sticks while recording in Chicago.

segments.title: Drummers with Oliver, Morton and Hilaire; Jeffery Tavern band
segments.summary: They discuss the drummer's employers and Hilaire, who played in Chicago with Jimmy Noone.

segments.title: Bass players, Johnny Lindsay, and New Orleans musicians who left young
segments.summary: Miller names New Orleans bassists, and they discuss Lindsay, Al Wynn and Simeon.

segments.title: How bass players got off: bowing and slapping; Louie Gallo
segments.summary: Miller describes a bassist who played with the end of the bow and a slap-style bassist on a record; they identify a pianist.

segments.title: Banjo players: Gallier, Lorenzo Staulz and the Marreros
segments.summary: Miller discusses banjoists he worked with and compares triple strokes with straight four.

segments.title: Bunk in New York and the New York jam session
segments.summary: They talk about seeing Bunk in New York, a jam session club and pay for three numbers.

segments.title: Hot and straight trumpet players, and the second Kid Punch band
segments.summary: Miller names the hot street musicians and straight readers, and tells of an imitator called second Kid Punch.

segments.title: More reading and get-off musicians; an unnamed teacher; tape end
segments.summary: Miller talks about Kaza and band leaders but cannot recall a teacher's name before the tape runs out.
